reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
clinicalPearls: A rare non-atherosclerotic cause of claudication in which a mucin-containing cyst within the arterial adventitia compresses the lumen; the popliteal artery is by far the commonest site.
Characteristically affects relatively young or middle-aged men without conventional cardiovascular risk factors.
Produces intermittent, sometimes rapidly progressive, calf claudication, with symptoms that may vary with knee position.
Ishikawa's sign describes loss of a palpable distal pulse on knee flexion as the cyst compression increases.
Imaging shows smooth extrinsic narrowing, the 'scimitar' sign on angiography, or an eccentric well-defined cyst on ultrasound and MRI without atherosclerosis elsewhere.
MRI is particularly useful, demonstrating the cystic fluid collection within the vessel wall.
Treatment is surgical, by cyst evacuation or resection with bypass or interposition graft; simple aspiration has a high recurrence rate.
It should be considered in any young patient with claudication and otherwise normal, non-atherosclerotic arteries.
reference.pathophysiology: A mucinous, gelatinous cyst resembling a ganglion develops within the adventitia of the artery and progressively encroaches on the lumen. Several origins are proposed: a developmental theory invoking embryonic mesenchymal rests, a degenerative ganglion-like process, and an articular theory in which a communication with the adjacent knee joint capsule allows synovial-type mucin to track along vascular branches into the adventitia. The cyst content is a mucopolysaccharide-rich fluid. Because the underlying problem is extrinsic compression of an otherwise healthy artery, symptoms depend on cyst volume and the position-dependent geometry of the vessel, and complete luminal thrombosis can occur.
additionalDifferentials: Extrinsic compression by a soft-tissue mass
additionalInvestigations: Ankle-brachial pressure index, which may fall with knee flexion or exercise
Duplex ultrasound showing an eccentric cystic wall lesion with a preserved distal artery
MRI or MR angiography, which best demonstrates the adventitial cyst and its content
Catheter angiography showing a smooth 'scimitar' or hourglass narrowing
Provocative positional testing of pulses and pressures
Histology of the resected cyst to confirm the diagnosis
redFlags: Acute limb ischaemia from complete arterial occlusion or thrombosis.
Rapidly worsening short-distance claudication or rest pain.
Loss of distal pulses, especially provoked by knee flexion.
New sensory or motor changes in the foot.
Recurrence of symptoms after previous treatment.
reference.prognosis: Outcomes after surgical treatment are generally good, with resolution of symptoms, although recurrence is well recognised, particularly after aspiration alone or when a joint communication is not addressed. Long-term patency is favourable when the diseased segment is resected and reconstructed.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as ordinary atherosclerotic claudication and missing the extrinsic cause in a young patient.
Relying on simple cyst aspiration, which is prone to recurrence.
Failing to recognise an associated communication with the knee joint.
Attempting angioplasty or stenting of an extrinsic compressive lesion, which tends to fail.
Confusing it with popliteal entrapment or a thrombosed aneurysm without dedicated cross-sectional imaging.
